evidence: Phaedr. 4.25.16–21: cum opus est, nīl habēs
terms.comment: The plain word for having a thing. It does not stretch as far as English “have”: one does not habēre a meal, a bath, a baby or a look; Latin names the action (prandēre, lavārī, parere, aspicere).

terms.grammar: phrase: the owner in the dative, the thing owned as the subject of esse
evidence: Mart. 11.18.2: rūs est mihi majus in fenestrā
terms.comment: As common as habeō, and the usual way with family, a name and qualities: est mihi frāter, I have a brother; nōmen mihi est …, my name is …

phrases.latin: dōnāstī, Lupe, rūs sub urbe nōbīs; sed rūs est mihi majus in fenestrā
phrases.english: you gave me a farm outside town, Lupus; but I have a bigger farm in my window

phrases.latin: nihil labōrās? ideō, cum opus est, nīl habēs
phrases.english: you do no work? That is why you have nothing when you need it

sources: Lewis & Short: habeo · Lewis & Short: sum
